utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't have the e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everybody in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. May I have the appearances.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Matthew Olmsted, Belinda Pidwell, Alexander Stevens, and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Eugene O'Sullivan for Stanisic Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic, Igor Pantelic, and Aleksandar Aleksic for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Before the witness takes the stand, we announce that we accept the proposal that was articulated yesterday by Ms. Pidwell of the OTP reflecting the consensus that was arrived at between OTP and the Defence, and that is for the adjournment of the trial to prepare the Witness 197 for cross-examination. And we also grant the motion for leave to amend the Rule 65 ter list and to add three videos for this witness, and also for the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And the amended summary. Thank you. So could the usher please escort the witness back to the stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, while the witness is coming in, I want to make a note that we would like to show this witness today the video P1563, just a small portion of it. This was mentioned in his proofing note, but we inadvertently left it off the list of proposed exhibits for this witness, and I hope that doesn't cause any problems. But as I said, it will just be a limited portion of that video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, good morning -- Kovacevic, good morning to you, sir. We are about --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: -- to continue your testimony. And before Mr. Olmsted resumes, I remind you you're still on your oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we have Exhibit 2D71 back on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you may recall that at the end of yesterday we were looking at this police file for the murder of eight persons by an unknown perpetrator. And if we take a look at this one-page criminal report, it states in essence that on 8 August 1992 eight bodies with visible injuries were found on the right bank of the Vrbas River. When you received this criminal report, did you have any information regarding where these murders had taken place?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we did not have any such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what about information regarding who the victims were or where they were from?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, we did not have that kind of information as to where the victims were from. The only thing we did know was that those were bodies of unidentified males.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, upon receiving this criminal report, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The criminal report was received and was forwarded in line with Article 156(2) [sic] for further criminal processing. That means that it was sent back to the police with instructions to perform other investigative and operative measures to uncover the perpetrators, co-perpetrators, any persons who may have issued orders for the crime to be committed, or any other persons who may have been involved in the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's turn to page 19 of the B/C/S version of this document, page 22 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you recognise this letter?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I believe you've just explained, generally, that you sent the criminal case back to the police. Is the purpose of this letter, therefore, to ask them to continue to engage in operative measures to identify the perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In line with Article 153, as stated here, not 156 - so it's just a correction - and this memo, what it says, it's correct. And this memo was then sent to the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, this memo, dated 10 September 1992 -- well, let me ask you this procedural question: Was it necessary for you to send this request before the police could begin measures to identify the perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This memo was necessary because the criminal report that had been submitted to the public prosecutor's office stated that the perpetrator of the crime was unidentified. The crime was the crime defined in Article 36 of the Criminal Code, and that required, under law 153(2) of the Law on Criminal Procedure adopted from the former Yugoslavia, to proceed in this manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, let me rephrase my question. I'm trying to get at something slightly different. As a procedural matter, was it necessary for the police to receive a request from you before they actually begin operative measures to identify a perpetrator, or could they have done that without any request from you?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police does its work continually in their effort to uncover -- identify the perpetrators and also to detect any other information pertaining to the perpetrators and the crime itself. It is the basic task of the police. Let me then make it clear. The police are there to identify the perpetrators of crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Why couldn't you open a criminal investigation in this case at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the laws valid at the time, the Law on Criminal Procedure, it was impossible to issue requests for an investigation against unidentified perpetrators of crimes. Under the law and regulations in force at the time, the powers were divided between various organs so that we had three organs, three types of powers: The organs who were in charge of uncovering crimes, the police and the investigative judges; then prosecutorial organs, the responsible public prosecutors' offices; and judicial organs issuing judgements. The courts, in other words. So a request to institute an investigation was a document that could be filed only by the prosecutor against known perpetrators of crimes. To be more specific, individually identified perpetrators. They had to have a full name; father's name; nickname; ethnic background, or perhaps they didn't have an ethnicity; the place of residence; criminal record, if any; the specification of crimes for which that person had been convicted; employment status; marital status; and so on. So all those personal details of the person that had to be specified in the pre-criminal proceedings, the proceedings in which appropriate information was gathered in the course of the operative work of the police, and this was something that the police did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's turn to page 11 of the B/C/S, page 12 of the English. What we have in front of us is a letter from CSB Banja Luka to the basic prosecutor's office, dated 14 September 1992, and it encloses three Official Notes of interviews as well as photographs of where the bodies in this case were found. First I want to draw your attention to the handwriting in the upper right-hand corner. We see it's written: "NN Prijedor - Skender Vakuf bodies." Can you tell us whether this is a reference to the killings at Koricanske Stijene?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who wrote this, this part of the document that's handwritten in this memo, so I can't really say anything as to what this refers to and when it was actually written, subsequently or at the time when the memo itself was either written or received. So I can't really tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you tell us, was this written by someone in your office or would it have been by someone in the police?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was not written by anyone from my office. The abbreviations and markings were not used by my office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, I don't understand fully what makes you suggest that this letter would have anything to do with Koricanske Stijene, and -- and more generally, perhaps, I fail to understand where we're going with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think that will be clear through the course of this testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, if we can look at the three pages that follow this 14 September letter, page 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page in both B/C/S and English. We see one of the Official Notes. If we can go to the next page to show the other one. And, finally, the third one, which is page 14 in B/C/S, page 15 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, we see before us, or we've seen now the three referenced Official Notes of interviews, and the first two were compiled on the 14th of September, 1992, and they were taken from two Prijedor police officers, Bosko Grabez and Vladimir Sobot, and one which was compiled on the 7 August 1992, taken of a police officer working a check-point.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, if we can go back two pages to page 12 of the B/C/S, page 13 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The two -- well, actually, all three interviews we can see were conducted on the 7th of August, 1992. In other words, a day before the on-site investigation took place. First of all, can you confirm: Did you receive these Official Notes from CSB Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if they were attached to the criminal report, then they reached the office of the prosecutor. I think they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, I should have asked you, actually: With regard to the 14 September letter that we had looked at just a while ago from CSB Banja Luka to the basic prosecutor's office, it references these Official Notes as well as photographs. Are these the three Official Notes that came with that 14 September letter?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, if we look at this statement by Grabez, we see that he stated he was escorting a convoy of 18 buses from Omarska to Manjaca on 6 August 1992, and then he further states that when they arrived at Manjaca, the persons on the bus were made to spend the night on the bus, and the next morning Grabez was told that several of these persons had died on the buses during the night. Mr. Kovacevic, upon receiving this Official Note, was this the first time that you learned that the victims were detainees from Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This Official Note indicated the possibility that those persons who had been brought in from the Prijedor municipality might be the ones, the ones that were -- had been brought to Manjaca. So the Official Note of a preliminary interview indicated that it might have been those persons who had brought -- who had been brought in from Prijedor to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Given that these interviews took place on the 7th of August, do you know why the police did not submit them with their 26 August criminal report?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Calling for speculation. Maybe you can rephrase that question. How this witness can know exactly what is going in the operative staff? So you can rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, if you know, do you know why, these Officials Notes or the interviews that took place on 7 August 1992 were not included with the 26 August criminal report? If you know.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really don't know why it was not included. I don't want to speculate. I could share my thoughts with you, but that would be just it. I really don't know why.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm really sorry. I believe you -- you -- your question, Mr. Olmsted, was that -- that these interviews took place on the 7th of August. Are you referring to this Official Note? It was the 14th of September. The date of this Official Note is 14th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. We see that the Official Note is dated 14 September, but if we read through the body of the text, it states that the interviews were conducted on the 7th of August, 1992. It's in the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, other than these three --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. If -- okay. Sorry, sorry. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, do you recall receiving any other witness statements from the police relating to this crime?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I can remember. I don't remember there were any other Official Notes or reports. This Official Note is the only thing that exists that accompanied this report of these interviews by the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, upon receiving these -- the photographs, which we don't have in front of us, and these three Official Notes, did you have sufficient information to open a criminal investigation in this case?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. As I said a moment ago, this was a criminal complaint against an unidentified perpetrator, and it was impossible to submit a request for an investigation to the competent investigating judge because the perpetrator was not identified. One could not carry out an investigation, according to the legislation in force then, against an unknown person.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Until you received the information about the identities of the perpetrators, what further actions as a prosecutor could you take in this case?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If an on-site investigation had been done, and I believe it was done in this case, we had to wait for the report on the on-site investigation, and I believe that in the criminal complaint it was mentioned that the investigating judge from the relevant lower court would perform it, so that de facto we had to wait for the protocol of the on-site investigation as a piece of evidence for some future proceedings that the prosecutor would start against identified perpetrators. As for some special powers of the prosecutor, apart from his ability to ask for further operative work to identify the criminal, there were none.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did you ever receive information from the police concerning the identities of the perpetrators of this crime?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did you -- did you ever receive information from the police regarding the identities of the victims of this crime?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I seem to remember that we received from the police, in fact, from the investigating judge, a protocol of the on-site investigation and photo documentation and a report on the external examination of the bodies. We received that from the investigating judge, and in that case it was, I believe, Mr. Djordje Stojakovic. I remember that because Djordje Stojakovic, the judge, worked in the criminal department of the lower court of Banja Luka at the time. So we received that protocol and the other documents from the investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, but yesterday we looked at the on-site investigation report and at least one of those expert examinations, and you may recall they do not mention the identities of the victims, and my question to you is whether you recall receiving any information regarding the names and other identification information about the victims.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regarding the identity of victims, as part of the expert report from the examination of the bodies, I believe there was also a report on the papillary lines of these victims, that is, finger-prints. And I believe the operative work thereafter continued, and I believe the investigating judge, Djordje Stojakovic, gave that documentation to the prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, let's look at page 3 of the of B/C/S. And I think this would be page 4 of the English. And what we have in front of us is one of the expert reports, and it's dated 8 August 1992. And can you confirm with us -- can you confirm for us that it does not provide any identification information regarding the victims?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the protocol on the forensic examination of an unidentified body. This record does not give any indication of identity. This is an investigative step carried out by a forensic specialist, a doctor, who lists the basic findings from the examination of the body, including injuries, if any, wounds, et cetera, and the confirmation of death, including rigor, which is one of the basic characteristics of a dead body. Here we see his findings on skeletal characteristics, four stabs and sharp edges. Four stab wounds with sharp edges.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you. You've answered the question. And we certainly can take a look -- closer look at this document at a later stage. I want to refresh your recollection with regard to what was in the prosecutor's office file in 1992, and to do that I want to show you 65 ter 10497, and I want us to turn to page 6 of the B/C/S and page 7 of the English. We see in this letter dated 26 November 2007, a list of documents comprising the prosecutor's office file as of 2007. So this is, of course, after the district prosecutor inherited this case. And we see there's a list of documents that were in the file, and with the exception of the interviews conducted in 2007, all the remaining documents are the ones we've already talked about; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. Maybe I'm wrong. 65 ter 10497, actually, this document, we -- do we have a ruling about the -- that document, that it is granted for admission to 65 ter list, because I have note here that it's pending Trial Chamber decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not tendering this into evidence. I'm using it simply to refresh this witness's recollection as to what was in the prosecutor's office file.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, I don't think that it's appropriate way to refresh memory with document that is not allowed to use. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, we've been through this several times during this trial, and the Trial Chamber has held that we can refresh the recollection of a witness with a document that is not necessarily on our 65 ter list. We obviously do not tender the document into evidence itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: That, too, is my recollection, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In any case, Your Honour, for the record I put my objection to this decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. So, Mr. Kovacevic, please take a look at this -- this letter listing what was in the prosecutor's office case file as of 2007. And with the exception of the interviews that were conducted in 2007, the remaining documents are those that we've already talked about; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: There's no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, should this arise again, of course you would phrase your question more carefully, because you ended up putting the question in a way that gave substance to Mr. Pantelic's objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And having reviewed this letter, does that refresh your recollection whether you received information, whether finger-print or otherwise, regarding the identity of the victims?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for these documents that were received by the public district prosecutor's office, they're all listed one by one: The criminal report, official notes from 14 September, record on the on-site investigation, official notes. May I just finish, if you don't mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection. Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- this is a document compiled subsequently. The witness had never seen it before. He's just reading it. How can he help the Court establish what happened in between, in between 1992 and some other point in time when he was not involved in the case? How did he know what was in the case file of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, the intervention that Mr. Pantelic had made earlier to which you responded and in respect of which the Chamber agreed with you, what we would have said in the past is certainly not a means or a device for getting the evidence in which otherwise cannot be admitted, and I agree with Mr. Krgovic that what we have here is a recitation of the witness from -- from the document which is, at this point, inadmissible.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, and I agree with that. My intention was not to have the witness read out the document. It was -- my question was whether -- I'll ask it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Whether having looked at this document, does that refresh your recollection as to whether you, when you handled this case, received any information regarding the identities of the victims.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already mentioned the finger-prints and the identity of the bodies. Whether all this pertained to this case or some other case, I really cannot confirm now with any certainty, but somehow it -- it's in my memory somewhere that there was this report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, it seems you've taken this as far as you could. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's fine. Now, based on your experience as a prosecutor, what additional operative measures should the police have taken to identify the perpetrators in this case?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police had to find all the operative information regarding the perpetrators of a specific crime. That would include getting citizens, various authorities, institutions, other police stations, and the army to give them any information they had about the possible identity of the perpetrators. At any rate, under the Law on Internal Affairs and the Law on Criminal Procedure, they had to continue working on identifying the perpetrators. Now, as for the concrete steps of the police, technical and other, the police knows very well what they have to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Would you have expected them to interview other persons who were on the buses where the victims allegedly died to find out more information about this case?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly one of those operative technical steps was to gather information on the identity of the perpetrators, and that would include taking statements from other people who are in any way involved in that convoy or that event directly or indirectly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If the police had provided you with information concerning the identity of the perpetrators, would there have been any reason for you to delay opening an investigation in this case?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had no reason to drag our feet. Once the identity of the perpetrators was identified following the regular procedure, then according to the Law on Criminal Procedure, the public prosecutor's offers would be legally obliged to submit a request [Realtime transcript read in error "question"] for an investigation against these persons and address it to the competent investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's move to Exhibit P1567.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we can go to page 2 in both the B/C/S and English. And if we can go to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. Just a short correction to the answer which is on the page 15, line 25. Instead of word "question for an investigation," I think the appropriate term should be "request for an investigation." [B/C/S spoken] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Is that correct, Mr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] That is correct. [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, what we have in front of us is the prosecutor's office case file for the killing of a number of persons at Koricanske Stijene on 21 August, 1992, by unknown perpetrators. In 1992, were you familiar with this case?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, I didn't know about this case in the broader sense of the word, but I learned of the case in end August 1992. I learnt there was an incident that happened in the area of what was then Skender Vakuf municipality, and I was informed by the basic public prosecutor, who said that this case would be entrusted to me to work on it once we received the criminal report.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what we have in front of us is the criminal report. This is the unknown perpetrator criminal report dated 8 September 1992. Can you confirm this is the report you received?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we can have 65 ter 2957 on the screen, page 27. If we could have page 27. And if we could zoom in on the right-hand side and -- into entry 2293. I'm sorry, the left-hand side. I don't know my left from my right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we look at entry 2293, can you confirm that this is the entry for this case?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the note about this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And just for the record, this is the Banja Luka Basic Prosecutor's Office KTN log-book.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, if we look in column 2, which is the date that the report would be received, we see a checkmark; but if we look two entries above, we see the date 11 September 1992. Is that when you received the report?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we can look at column 17 for this entry, we see the date 30 August 1999. Can you tell us what happened at that date?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day, the entire case file was submitted by the public prosecutor's office to the district prosecutor's office in Banja Luka because actual jurisdiction had changed between the courts and automatically also between the prosecutors' offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this exhibit be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1574, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's return to P1567, page 2. Now, prior to receiving this report, had you received any documentation in this case?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What about an on-site investigation report?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Prior to receiving this criminal report, had you seen or heard anything in the media regarding this crime?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have any knowledge whatsoever, apart from the information that was very terse that I received from my boss, Mr. Nebojsa Pantic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could look at the last page of this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Which is -- if we could turn the page. No, we had it; now it went away. There we go. And the English as well. Turn another page. Turn to the last page of this particular document. I think it's -- there we are. Page 3 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We see at the end of this criminal report there is a list of attachments, and the first attachment is a set of official notes of interviews. The second is a list of names of some of the victims. The third is personal documents of some of the victims, and the fourth is a special report from the command of the 22nd Light Infantry Brigade, dated 21 August 1992. I want to talk first about the first set of attachments, the official notes of interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could turn to the next page in both the B/C/S and the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you recall receiving the official notes along with the criminal report?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A certain number of those notes did come in with the criminal report, ten or maybe more. Those were statements gathered in the course of preliminary interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What about the official notes of interviews with Cedo Milovanovic and Radoslav Brkic, the two reserve police officers from SJB Skender Vakuf? Do you recall receiving those with the criminal report?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether those official notes of interviews were attached. I allow that they might have been, the possibility that they might have been attached.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's look at page 12 of the B/C/S, page 14 of the English. And this is a list of persons from the Prijedor-Travnik convoy from 21 August 1992, assumed to have been killed. Do you recall seeing this list of victims back in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was attached to the criminal report.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were you ever informed by the police that the bodies of women and children were also found at the crime scene?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police did not inform me, nor did any other organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's turn to page 14 of the B/C/S, page 16 of the English. And this is a report from the command of the 22nd Light Infantry Brigade, dated 21 August 1992. And I note for the record that there's a typographical error in the English version. In the header it should read "Confidential Number 13/1," not "43/4."

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, is this the military report that accompanied the criminal report?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, it was attached. This document was attached to the criminal report too.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: It states that the Prijedor and Sanski Most police were escorting the convoy and that police members participated in the liquidation. Does this report make it clear to you that the civilian police were the perpetrators of this crime?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, objection. It's calling for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I would have thought the objection would have been, "Does it matter?" We have the document. The witness may have his views, but the document speaks for itself. What -- he may have an interpretation which others may not share, but it's a document that -- on which you're concentrating, I would have thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, I don't know whether this is of any importance, but because you were mentioning it, the number on the English version seems to me 43/4, the same as on the B/C/S version. What's your basis to say that this is an error?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The basis is that when we looked at the attachments to the criminal report, it actually references a document with the number 13/1, and these -- on the B/C/S version of this document in front of us, those 1s -- those 4s -- well, it could either be a 1 or a 4, and so I was just noting that I think that that might be the error. But perhaps you're right. Perhaps you're right. Perhaps they are 4s and in the criminal report it's wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: They are certainly 4s because there are 1s in line in "1997." The year, for instance, you see what the 1 is, and it's definitely 43/4.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Then the typographical error is in the criminal report itself then. I stand corrected on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Olmsted, it might be some other document as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, finally, the criminal report referenced personal documents of the victims. Do you recall what kinds of personal documents were recovered from the victims that you were able to see?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that a certain number of personal documents belonging to the victims had come in, and they happened to be stored in the premises of the basic court because there were no storage facilities in the basic public prosecutor's office where the documents and items belonging to those persons could be stored. Those were items of clothing, ID cards, partially destroyed medical insurance cards, some family photographs, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's turn to page 15 of the B/C/S, page 17 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And this is a letter from the Banja Luka Basic Prosecutor's Office to the basic court dated 14 September 1992. Can you tell us, did you write this letter to Investigative Judge Jevto Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You submit this question pursuant to Article 156 of the Law on Criminal Procedure. Can you tell us, just very briefly, what is the purpose of that particular article?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The essence of this article -- or, rather, of what I did pursuant to this article is my assessment as a prosecutor that this is an investigative action that must be taken without delay. In practice, this meant that those were persons who had been victims of a crime. They were also members of another ethnic community. And in order to protect the victims, in order to ensure that the perpetrators are prosecuted criminally in the future, that they should be -- that the victims should be heard by the investigative judge. And also, those persons, because they were from the municipality of Prijedor, could, in their statements to the investigative judge, provide information about the perpetrators of the crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So to be clear, you're not requesting for a -- a criminal investigation to be opened by the investigative judge here; this is a pre-investigation measure?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. We cannot open an investigation because the perpetrators were unknown, unidentified, as I've already indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, in your letter you recommend that the investigative judge question eight persons who were interviewed by the police. Were these eight persons the survivors of the crime?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My intention under Article 156 was precisely to ensure that those people, victims, the injured parties in the event, could be heard or questioned as part of this investigative action.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's look at page 16 of the B/C/S, page 19 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What we're looking at now is a letter from the Banja Luka Basic Court, and in particular Judge Jevto Jankovic, to the Banja Luka Basic Prosecutor's Office, and it's dated 24 September 1992. Do you recall receiving this letter?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, attached to this letter and included in this case file in the pages that follow this letter are five records of interviews of survivors of the Koricanske Stijene killings, and they're dated either the 16th or 17th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could just turn to the next page in both documents, both English and the B/C/S, so we can see an example of one of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: They all indicate that you attended the interviews. Do you recall attending these interviews?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did attend most of them. I can't remember specifically attending all of them. I may have been present at the beginning and then I was called away because I had other tasks, ongoing trials and other work of a deputy public prosecutor. So in some cases I would be there just to begin. I would be there at the beginning of the interview, and then I was called away. Or in some other cases I may have attended the whole interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you recall where the interviews took place?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The interviews took place in the office of the investigative judge, Mr. Jevto Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you tell us, how did the victims or the survivors appear during these interviews?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the victims looked exhausted, really very fatigued. They also looked scared. And they looked ill, to put it mildly, exhausted. It was obvious that they needed medical care and other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Other than the five survivors that you interviewed with Judge Jankovic, did you conduct -- you or the judge conduct any other interviews of either survivors or any other witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have a basis under the law to actually interrogate anyone in this stage, the pre-indictment stage in the proceedings when the prosecutor does not play an active role under the legislation in force at the time. And the prosecutor's role at this stage in the proceedings where there will be criminal proceedings down the road is minimal or, in fact, nonexistent. So I could ask questions in the office of the investigative judge, Jevto Jankovic, only subject to his approval, and I could attend the investigative actions when invited by him, just to give you an example.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now -- now, based on these interviews by the investigative judge, were you able to open a criminal investigation?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was unable to do so for the reasons that I've already mentioned because the perpetrators of the crime had not been identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's take a look at page 29 of the B/C/S, page 30 of the English. This is a letter dated 30 September 1992 from the basic public prosecutor's office to CSB Banja Luka. Do you recall sending this letter to the police?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And we looked at a similar letter with regard to the case involving the killings outside of Manjaca camp. Was the purpose of this letter the same?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did you ever receive information from the police in response to your letter?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's look at page 46 of the B/C/S, page 58 of the English. And this is a letter from CSB Banja Luka to the district public prosecutor's office dated 11 November 1999. And if we could just leave where we are in the B/C/S version but turn the page in the English. Well, we don't have the English on the screen yet. But as soon as we do. We need page 58 in English. Yes, this is the right document. Now, if we can turn to the second page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We can see in this letter that the CSB reports that: "... by checking the protocol books, we have determined that the request of the Banja Luka Public Prosecutor's Office number KTN-2293/92 of 30 September 1992 has been received by the centre, but action was not taken in accordance with it nor was any report on collecting the necessary information submitted to the Banja Luka Public Prosecutor's Office." So is that consistent with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's bring up on the screen P618.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is a memorandum from SJB Prijedor chief Simo Drljaca to the chief of the CSB Banja Luka, dated 13 October 1992, and in this document Chief Drljaca states that he provided the CSB chief with a list of police officers who escorted the Trnopolje convoy in document number 11-12-16, dated 22 September 1992, which is eight days before you returned the case file to CSB Banja Luka. He also provides the names of two police officers who provided traffic security, Vladimir Sobot and Bosko Grabez, who we also saw gave statements with regard to the Manjaca camp killings on 6 August 1992. Were you provided with any of this information?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see this document. I did not receive it at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But the information contained within it regarding the persons that Chief Drljaca had identified, did you receive that information?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not receive that information either. So the prosecution simply did not have any information relating to the persons listed here in this memo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, this would be a good time, I think, for the break, if I move on to another issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, just for the record, Mr. Cvijetic joined us at the very beginning of the first session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we may have P1567 back on the screen. And if we can turn to page 38 of the B/C/S, page 45 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What we have before us is the official note of an interview of crime technician Radovan Sukalo, dated 4 October 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could turn to the next page in the English only.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to draw your attention to the point in his statement where he states: "As far as I can remember, an investigating judge did not join us ..." And he's talking about when the team -- the crime technician team came to the crime scene at Koricanske Stijene. Mr. Kovacevic, was it real procedure to conduct crime scene forensic work outside the presence of an investigative judge?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the Law on Criminal Procedure in effect at the time, the legal possibility existed that an investigating judge who had been informed about the existence of elements of a certain crime and that he should come out to the crime scene, the possibility existed that he do not go there himself but instead to transfer, to assign his powers to police workers.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you know if that's what happened in this case?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, that's not what happened in this case. From what I know, the investigating judge did not issue an authorisation that certain persons should take steps regarding an on-site investigation. Perhaps he gave that authorisation verbally, but I'm not aware of any written order.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you explain to us why it was standard practice for an investigative judge to be present during on-site forensic work at the crime scene?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under our legislation, the investigating judge is an institution within the legal system, within the judicial system, that is in charge of leading an investigation or conducting an investigation, together with internal affairs organs or other organs, and taking steps that are necessary to shed light on a crime due to the urgency of the matter, the urgency of gathering information, securing the crime scene, et cetera. And therefore, the investigating judge had the powers to conduct investigative actions with a view to providing evidence for future prosecutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So if I understand your answer correctly, at least one of the reasons why an investigative judge is present at the crime scene is to make sure that the evidence obtained is secured and handled properly.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If I may clarify. The presence of the investigating judge is important, precisely because of the fact that he provides for and orders the seizure of documents and persons and the taking of statements on the scene, and such statements have the weight of evidence per se, and all these elements made it incumbent upon the investigating judge to be present at the on-site investigation and to provide a protocol, the minutes, the records of that investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have an objection to this entire line of questioning. The Prosecutor misleads the witness. He presents -- he puts certain things before him and then leads him to certain answers. He can instead show documents about an investigation on site, the presence of the investigating judge and what he did, but instead he puts before him a document showing that the investigating judge wasn't there and then asks him why it is important for the investigating judge -- wasn't there -- or why his role is important. This is a waste of time, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And in addition, if I may add that I do not think, Mr. Olmsted, that you need to explain to this Court why the presence of an investigative judge is necessary on the crime scene. So I think you should move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. But in response to the objection, I was not asking the witness whether this statement was true or not; I was just asking him with regard to the procedure. But as I understand, the Trial Chamber understand the procedure. I'm just going to move to one other point on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: A little bit further down, Sukalo states that video footage and photographs were taken at the scene. Were you aware of this in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard, informally, that certain investigating actions had taken place on the scene. Whether that was filming or photographing, I cannot be sure. I cannot be sure that I heard it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's play --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say that I knew about it. I didn't know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's play P1563. This is a video that has been played already, and I want to queue it to 55 minutes and 48 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: First of all, can you identify that this is the area of Koricanske Stijene? I'm sorry. I will repeat my question. Mr. Kovacevic, can you confirm that -- can you identify this area as Koricanske Stijene?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise to my friend. Maybe -- maybe the proper way would be ask first of all to ask him whether this witness was ever at the location and then to -- to identify it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I can ask that. Yes. First of all, just pause it for now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, can you tell us, did you ever go to the crime scene at Koricanske Stijene?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never been there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you, as you look at this video, can you identify whether this area that's being depicted is Koricanske Stijene?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, no go. The witness hasn't been there. Move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, do you know whatever happened to the bodies the police recovered at Koricanske Stijene?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what happened to the bodies. I heard informally that attempts had been made to recover the bodies. How, on what occasion, I don't know. It's what I heard, informally.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, today we've looked at two case files that you worked on in 1992 in which a number of non-Serbs were victims. In both cases you submitted a request to the police to identify the perpetrators, and you did not receive responses. How would you describe the police's lack of responsiveness to your efforts to shed light on these and other such cases?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question sounds simple, but the answer requires a small introduction, with your leave. The general situation in the territory of Bosnian Krajina was wartime, de facto wartime. A huge number of refugees from municipalities affected by the war, territories that later came to constitute the federation, general poverty, lack of the basic necessities, no electricity, large numbers of reservists passing through the town on their way to the front line and back, reserve policemen also, frequent shootings. The general backdrop was such that in hindsight it's difficult to give a straight, simple answer to your question. Could you repeat that specific question?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. How would you describe the lack of responsiveness to your request for additional information to identify the perpetrators from the police? What did you feel you were confronted with?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in certain situations with some people, you were faced with a wall of silence from the police for various objective or subjective, real or personal circumstances that I was not able to go into at the time or to justify. Some part of this wall of silence could be perhaps understandable because of the fact that a large number of people who could be potential perpetrators of such crimes from other municipalities did not fall until -- under our jurisdiction, which was locality based, territory based. We had jurisdiction over Banja Luka, Prijedor, Prnjavor, Gradiska; so that with this constant turnover of policemen, soldiers, civilians, the influx of refugees who had or didn't have a wartime assignment and the lack of ability to register all these people, all this led to incidents where you couldn't determine where these people had come from, from Banja Luka town or from Banja Luka municipality or from Prijedor municipality or some other municipality. So I suppose that as far as the identification of certain perpetrators is concerned and all the operative and technical work and in the communication between various authorities, primarily police authorities, there arose the issue of jurisdiction. For example, there were several cases when the jurisdiction of certain prosecutorial offices from Prijedor clashed with jurisdictions in Banja Luka or Gradiska. Once it is discovered that the perpetrators came from a certain territory, for reasons of judicial economy or other reasons, the case would be given to the office in Gradiska or Prnjavor, et cetera. I'm trying to say that precisely from the territory of Prijedor municipality, when cases like these two happened and in some other cases that did not involve crimes of this nature, you sometimes came up against this wall of silence, and the perpetrators remained unidentified.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to show you --

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, let me just finish. I can't say that this wall of silence was a common occurrence in the CSB Banja Luka. With certain authorities from the CSB Banja Luka we had a good co-operation, good quality work, but with people who came from other municipalities or people about whom we didn't know where they came from, whether they were members of the army or the police, we didn't know whether they were regular soldiers or regular policemen or reserve policemen, it sometimes remained unknown because it was difficult to get access to all this information. And that's why I could understand in certain circumstances why this wall of silence arose, although I couldn't justify it in -- in -- from the aspect of -- of criminal investigation work.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's take a look at 2D72. What we have in front of us is a criminal case against Radomir Boskan, amongst others. Are you familiar with this case?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in part.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were you aware that these perpetrators were members of the Banja Luka Special Police Detachment?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware. I knew these persons by name. I'm not sure all of them were members of the police, but some of them who were recorded in the crime registers of the prosecutor's office were known to me as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Radomir Boskan, did he have a criminal record from before the conflict, so before April 1992?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember well, this man had some sort of criminal record. He had prior convictions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's take a look at P588.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't see the purpose of this examination. Maybe the witness can be asked whether he was involved in this case, whether he took any steps. Then maybe this question can continue. However, if he's shown newspaper articles or things that have nothing to do with his actual work, then I don't see what sort of assistance this can offer to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm only asking questions that are within the personal knowledge of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: To what end?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, most of my questions -- or the las few ones were foundational, to establish that he's at least aware of case. I'm not saying that he worked on this case. But I beg leave to ask my -- a few more questions so that you'll see where I'm going with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: You have done so a couple of times previously this morning, and as I recall, your promises were not fulfilled. Remember I asked you a question this morning about the importance of a document in which apparently by handwriting reference was made, perhaps, to the Koricanske Stijene incidents, and you promised me that that would become clear later on. It still is unclear to me, Mr. Olmsted. And, frankly, I feel that this is another example where we might not fully appreciate the reasons why you wish to pursue this -- this issue. But we'll allow you once again the chance, and we hope that you will keep your promise.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And I apologise. I thought it was clear through my examination, the point I was seeking to achieve. But perhaps that will be best reserved for argument at the end of the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, you have in front of you an article.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could zoom in on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And then it's -- the article's entitled: "An Unprecedented Case/A State Is Not Built by Violence." And it's dated 24 June 1992. Do you recall what happened to Boskan and other members of the special police detachment after their arrest?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that they were remanded in custody. I don't know what happened, and I don't know what arrest is referred to here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were you aware that there was an effort -- a successful effort to break them out of prison or the Tunjice gaol?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when this was going on, I was not in the public prosecutor's office. I had not yet been appointed the deputy public prosecutor. And I heard that there had been an incident that involved an attack on the prison, but I have next to no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's fine. I want to return to the two cases that you worked on involving unknown perpetrators, the Manjaca camp killing incident and, secondly, the Koricanske Stijene killing incident. Now, we saw from the documents we looked at that two traffic police officers were interviewed with regard to both of those incidents, and we also saw from the report from the light infantry brigade that there was at least a suspicion that the Prijedor police were involved in that crime, in the crime of Koricanske Stijene. At any time while you were the deputy prosecutor assigned to those cases, did the police come to you and inform you that the perpetrators of these crimes may be the same people?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police never notified me of anything of the sort. I did not have any knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Kovacevic. Mr. Kovacevic, how long did you work in the public prosecutor's office in total?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thirteen or fourteen years.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And tell me - I would like to clarify a few issues - it is a fact, is it not, that under the law in force in the territory of the former Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, and I'm referring first and foremost to the Law on Criminal Procedure, the role of the public prosecutor's office was -- one of its roles was to initiate criminal proceedings by issuing an indictment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When a criminal report was issued -- or, rather, when an indictment was issued, the prosecutor's office actually qualified the crime that the accused was charged with on the basis of the conclusions and evidence obtained in the course of the investigation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now, for this reason, the initial qualification of a crime in the criminal report was basically just some kind of a guidance for you as the prosecutor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In order to make things even more complicated, the Court, when it tries a person, is not bound to apply the same qualification that you applied for the accused; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your answer has not been recorded. Could you please state your answer.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The court is bound only by the description of facts from the indictment, not the qualification?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That would also be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And, in essence, it means that you file an indictment to the court for a crime of robbery, and in the course of the trial the court finds that it is, in fact, aggravated robbery and the court then convicts the accused of that crime; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, tell me, when you make your decision as a prosecutor how to qualify legally the offence in the initial indictment, you definitely have in mind the results of the investigation, in other words, all the information gathered in the course of the investigation, and in line with this information, you opt for the crime that you will charge the accused with in the indictment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I assume that in situations when the results of an investigation indicate that the borderline -- that it's a borderline case between two offences, the prosecutor would always charge the more serious crime. That was usual practice; right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was usual practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The gravity of a crime is a direct consequence of the gravity of the punishment envisaged by the law. Is that not so?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So if the law envisages the death penalty for a crime, it's the severest crime under the criminal law system in the former Yugoslavia, then it would be one of the most severest crimes; right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Page 38, line 1, "severest punishment," not "severest crime."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see that the interpreters have made a correction, but I really did say that it would be the most severe crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So let me get to the essence. If the crime of murder, first degree murder, involving a number of victims, low intents, and so on, for those -- for this type of crime, a death penalty was envisaged under the law?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So for you as a prosecutor, the decision whether to qualify a crime as first degree murder, which carried a penalty of death, or some other crime, for instance, war crime, which also carried the penalty of death, was -- it was all the same for the Prosecution in terms of the gravity of the crime?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for the basic public prosecutor's office in Banja Luka, we did not have any other crimes in practice which carried the death penalty apart from these ones. These were the only ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But at any rate, war crimes were in the jurisdiction of military prosecutors' offices?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Under the law adopted -- that was adopted from the former state, the Law on Military Courts and the Law on Criminal Procedure, I think that all war crimes and crimes against civilians were in the jurisdiction of military courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, sir, while you were a prosecutor before the events in the 1990s, before the conflict broke out, did you attend any seminars for -- organised for prosecutors? Did you follow law practice, case law, and so on?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, as a rule. I did not attend all of the training seminars, but quite a few of them I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that in pre-war Yugoslavia there was no case law for war crimes existed, and this topic had not been dealt with at any of the seminars organised for prosecutors?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was never discussed. That chapter in the Criminal Code that covered those crimes was not discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: My learned friend Mr. Olmsted asked you some questions, and now I would like to hear your opinion -- or, rather, what you as a prosecutor know. In the course of 1992, did the public prosecutor's office discriminate in any way in terms of dealing with criminal cases against anyone in terms of victims or perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The public prosecutor's office never did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When we're talking about this, I'm referring to the cases where a Serb committed a crime against non-Serbs as victims or injured parties. So was there any --

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was never any discrimination. No distinction was ever made in the work of the public prosecutor's office in relation to the victims or perpetrators, regardless of their ethnic background, religion, or any other kind of affiliation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, in the basic public prosecutor's office in Banja Luka, in addition to yourself and your superior, the prosecutor, you talked about him, there were other employees, and some of these people came from other ethnic communities, non-Serbs, in other words?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And that was in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992 and even afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We briefly touched upon the situation regarding the Military Prosecutor's Office. Do you know when the military court or the Military Prosecutor's Office in the 1st Krajina Corps in Banja Luka was actually established?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it happened sometime in early September 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I would now like to show you a document. It's P1328. That's at tab 71. This is a reminder sent by Momcilo Mandic, a justice minister, from 1992. You remember that Momcilo Mandic was the justice minister in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And this document is dated the 5th of August, 1992, and this letter is a supplement to another letter that was sent in July 1992 to the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, to the president, in fact, Dr. Radovan Karadzic, where the Justice Ministry again puts the initiative that until appropriate military judicial organs are set up, the appropriate civilian judicial organs should take over the jurisdiction of military judicial organs. Are you familiar with this initiative?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about this initiative in that time period, September or October. I heard about this initiative. I knew that it existed. But since at that time I had not yet been appointed deputy public prosecutor, it was in August, in fact. And then when I started my work, I heard that this initiative had been launched by the Justice Ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like the witness to look at P1318, item 23. So P1318, item 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's a report on the work of the Ministry of Justice and Administration for the period May to October 1992, and the date is the 16th of November, 1992. I don't know whether you've had an opportunity to look at this report.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I learnt about this report sometime in 1993, so I hadn't seen it before. It was at a time when the report on the activities of the basic public prosecutor's office was being drafted for 1992, and then I heard that there was a report of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So could we then look at page 2, the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume that it's also the same page in the English version. I apologise. It appears that I made a mistake. The English version should be page 3. Sir, you can see the last paragraph here. Yes. So in the English version that's the last paragraph. I think you can probably scroll down a little bit. Thank you very much. It begins with the words "Judicial organs."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And so the Justice Ministry says in its report: "The judicial organs do not perform their functions with equal efficiency and usefulness. The Supreme Court and the republican public prosecutor's office have not begun to work yet, since the relevant personnel has not been elected or appointed as yet, and the premises for these organs have not been secured." Sir, it runs over to the next page in Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The English text is fine as it is. Now could we please look at page 3 in the Serbian text for the benefit of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So, here, you can see it.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So is it your recollection that at that time, for the best part of 1992, because this is dated November 1992, that the republican public prosecutor's office had not yet been set up?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall in part. Not all of it, but some parts, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So the Supreme Court and the republican public prosecutor's office, the two highest judicial organs, have not begun to function by the 16th of November, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please look at page 3 -- or, rather, page 4 in -- both in Serbian and in English. Next page, in fact. We have to go to page 5 in the English language. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The first sentence on this page, it says: "Failure to set up military judicial bodies promptly." You see that?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: "The failure to set up the military judicial organs promptly makes it difficult for the rule of law to function properly, since in the current conditions it is mostly military courts and military prosecutor's offices that have jurisdiction over crimes because general mobilisation has been declared." And then it goes on to say - well, I am not going to read on - that the military judiciary is not up and running yet as it should, that this they do not have appropriate personnel, and that crimes from military jurisdiction are on the rise. And the initiative that we saw in August is relaunched here for the civilian courts to temporarily assume the jurisdiction of the military courts. Do you recall that the situation was like this, in fact?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I had some information about this initiative, that this initiative actually existed, but I did not have any other information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is a fact, however, that this initiative was rejected by the military and that you never took over any of the tasks from the purview of the military judiciary or military courts, not even temporarily?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that the military prosecutor of the Military Prosecutor's Office, at the command of the 1st Krajina Corps in Banja Luka, was captain Spasoje Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Pisarevic?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I met him on one occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like the witness to look at 1D00-0841.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is a letter sent by Mr. Pisarevic. The date is the 19th of September, 1992. And it was signed by him as military prosecutor. It is actually a report on crime trends and the work of the Military Prosecutor's Office. And then he says -- he's listing problems he's encountered in his work. The Military Prosecutor's Office was established pursuant to a decision of the 31st of May, 1992, but now by mid-September it does not have enough personnel to ensure proper functioning and conduct of proceedings. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I have the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You see on the second page it says: "Military prosecutor. "In view of the number of cases in the territory covered by this prosecutorial office, daily occurrences of various actions against the law that are subject to prosecution, I suggest that the Military Prosecutor's Office should expand to include at least six deputies."

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if they had any staffing problems?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know they did. I know that we did, and the Military Prosecutor's Office also had the same problems with personnel. And, once, we even discussed it, Prosecutor Pisarevic and I, from the basic public prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And then we see a review of crime trends. He quotes the number of criminal files inherited from before. He says that they referred 1573 cases to the jurisdiction of other prosecutor's offices. And then he says: "The remaining 3.327 cases, of which 820 criminal reports were not even recorded, are currently being dealt with." That means that out of 3.000-something criminal reports received, 820 were not even entered in their registers.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Look at page 3, briefly. The stamp and the signature of Mr. Pisarevic. Military Prosecutor, Captain Spasoje Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there is no objection, I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D367, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
